title: Aurelius Systems — Runtime performance deep dive (on-prem + hybrid)
summary: Redwood SE team walked Aurelius through GPU runtime tradeoffs for on-prem and hybrid deployment. Focus: kernel selection, CUDA graph stability, persistent KV cache behavior under eviction, quantization (int8 vs int4), batching policies, and secure VPC connectivity. Customer wants a pilot with latency SLO 50ms p95 for short-chat workloads and a plan for deterministic fallbacks if TensorRT paths become unavailable.

Lina: Schedule 2-hour pilot runbook session w/ Aurelius infra (proposed 2025-02-05)
Aurelius: Provide sample LLM traces and workload mix (chat 65%, embeddings 20%, rerank 15%)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-30 16:00 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Theo (Redwood SRE), Rebecca (Aurelius ML Infra), Marcus (Aurelius SRE), Eileen (Aurelius Security), Tomás (Aurelius Backend)

Summary (auto): Quick-run of runtime tradeoffs. Customer is evaluating an on-prem pilot with hybrid burst to Redwood hosted. Key constraints: 50ms p95 SLO for short-turn chats, encryption-at-rest with customer KMS, and deterministic fallbacks for model variant changes.

00:00:00 Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, and Lina will drive the deep dive.
00:00:20 Lina (Redwood SE): Hi, hello. I pulled together some perf runs comparing our TensorRT-LLM path against our vLLM-style path; also a few notes on cuda graph lifetime behavior with persistent KV caches. We'll go slow and answer infra questions as we go.
00:00:45 Rebecca (Aurelius): Great, we want to understand stability more than raw peak numbers. Our infra team cares about evictions and what happens mid-request if the Graph or kernel path falls back.
00:01:10 Lina: Cool. Top-level: for short chats (<=128 tokens) TensorRT-LLM with properly warmed CUDA graphs + persistent KV gives the lowest p95, usually ~30-60% lower than naive vLLM in our tests on A100 80GB. But that depends on kernel selection, quant, and the eviction policy.
00:02:05 Marcus: When you say "properly warmed", is that pre-warming the CUDA graphs per model? We have multi-tenant GPUs and can't pin graphs forever.
00:02:20 Lina: Right, good point. There are two patterns: ephemeral graphs per inference vs persistent graphs per model variant. Ephemeral reduces memory pressure but increases cold-start tail latency. Persistent graphs plus pinned kernel selection requires reserved capacity or dedicated GPUs.
00:02:55 Samir: We recommend a hybrid: keep a small LRU of persistent graphs for hot variants and fall back to an ephemeral vLLM-style runtime for cold variants. We have automated routing rules in Redwood that will route to the faster path and degrade gracefully.
00:03:30 Eileen (Aurelius): From a security perspective, if you persist graphs or caches on customer hardware, we need keys in our KMS and audit logs. How does Redwood integrate with HSM/KMS?
00:03:45 Theo (Redwood SRE): For Private deployments we support customer KMS via KMIP and cloud provider KMS integrations. Keys stay in the HSM and disk is encrypted; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll include the redwood-security-pack.pdf link in follow-up.
00:04:20 Tomás (Aurelius): On the quant front, what's your recommended default? We're trying to conserve memory on our on-prem 80GB nodes but want high fidelity.
00:04:35 Lina: int8 quant with per-channel calibration is our baseline for production; it gives a good balance. int4 can get you further memory reductions but is model-sensitive — hallucination risk increases for some instruction-tuned models. Our Optimize tool recommends quant profiles based on your eval set.
00:05:10 Rebecca: Do you have numbers for int8 vs int4 on small chat models?
00:05:20 Lina: On a 7B instr-tuned model we saw ~18% slower token time for int4 in the critical path due to additional dequant steps and sometimes kernel misses; memory drops about 40%. For 13B and up the benefits are larger, but again depends on kernel availability.
00:06:05 Marcus: Kernel availability?
00:06:10 Lina: Some TensorRT kernels are only available on certain architectures or for certain opsets. The runtime will attempt the highest-performance kernel and fall back to a generic CUDA kernel if not present, which increases latency. So kernel selection heuristics matter.
00:06:30 Samir: We capture that in our perf matrix per model: for each op and sequence length, which kernel wins. We'll share the spreadsheet.
00:07:00 Rebecca: About the persistent KV cache — what if the cache gets evicted mid-session due to memory pressure? Does the request fail or degrade?
00:07:15 Lina: Good question. Our system supports three strategies: 1) eviction with re-generation — we recompute the lost cache segments (costly), 2) on-disk spill — slower but deterministic, 3) immediate fallback to vLLM path that reconstructs context incrementally. We prefer 3 for availability: it keeps the request alive but incurs a latency penalty.
00:07:55 Marcus: Is there jitter or correctness drift between paths?
00:08:05 Lina: There can be small differences — especially with quantized kernels and non-deterministic fused ops. We track a reproducibility score and recommend running a small canary to check output parity; if parity drifts beyond threshold we force a model variant pin.
00:08:40 Rebecca: Can you control the LRU size for persistent graphs and KV caches? We need to tune for our mixed workload.
00:08:50 Lina: Yes, everything is configurable — LRU thresholds, spill policy, eviction priority by age vs by token-count. Our Optimize tool can suggest starting parameters based on sample traces.
00:09:20 Tomás: CUDA graphs — we noticed instability when replaying graphs across model versions; sometimes the graph is invalid if op shapes change. How do you detect/recover?
00:09:35 Lina: We version graphs tied to model version and sequence length profile. If the graph replays fail, our runtime invalidates it and falls back to the standard kernel path while queuing a graph recompile in the background.
00:10:05 Eileen: Do these falls get logged for audit? We need visibility into failed recompiles, who triggered them, and timestamps.
00:10:15 Theo: Yes, events for recompile/failure are emitted and collected in the console under model -> graph health. We can forward those to your Splunk/Datadog.
00:10:40 Marcus: For our pilot, we want to run a mixed workload with bursts to hosted Redwood for overflow. Can you explain routing when on-prem is saturated?
00:10:55 Samir: We have smart routing: priorities by latency SLO, cost, and policy. You can set rules to spill only certain traffic classes to hosted Redwood (non-sensitive data), or route everything to hosted but encrypt-at-rest with your keys. For PII workloads you can mark them as "no spill".
00:11:30 Rebecca: Latency SLO is 50ms p95 for short chats. Can you realistically achieve that with spillover and persistent graphs?
00:11:45 Lina: On properly provisioned hardware with warmed graphs, yes for short chats. If we have to spill to hosted we add network hop; we'd expect p95 to increase by ~20-40ms depending on region. So route policy matters.
00:12:20 Tomás: We also have operational constraints: we run BF16 models in some pipelines. How does that interact with quant and TensorRT kernels?
00:12:35 Lina: BF16 is simple and sometimes faster than mixed-precision FP16 on certain GPUs due to internal accumulation differences. TensorRT has strong FP16 paths; quant reduces memory but changes numeric behavior. We'll include per-model recommendations in the doc pack.
00:13:05 Speaker 6: (unclear) Does Redwood support per-route model pinning?
00:13:10 Samir: Yep. You can pin model versions per route and specify fallback variants.
00:13:30 Marcus: Can we get a runbook for debugging sudden tail-latency spikes? We need a triage checklist.
00:13:45 Lina: We'll share a triage checklist: check graph health, kernel fallbacks, GPU memory pressure, KV cache evictions, and recent rollout changes. Also trace correlation ids are exposed in the console so you can follow a single request through runtime.
00:14:15 Rebecca: About deterministic fallbacks — if a TensorRT kernel fails mid-request and we go to vLLM, do we get the same logits/hypotheses? We need reproducibility for evaluation.
00:14:30 Lina: Not guaranteed bitwise-equivalent. Different kernels and quant can yield slightly different logits. For evaluation you can pin an evaluation model variant and run offline batch comparisons. For production, we surface "regression alerts" when output drift exceeds configured thresholds.
00:15:05 Tomás: Any gotchas with CUDA graph replays on multi-GPU setups? We've seen hangs.
00:15:20 Lina: Multi-GPU with NCCL can be tricky: graph capture must account for cross-GPU comms. Our runtime captures per-device graph segments and a coordinator layer; hangs are typically due to mismatched shapes or unexpected NCCL timeouts when one device hasn't been warmed. We recommend gradually warming devices and avoiding full-simultaneous capture on heterogeneous GPUs.
00:15:55 Marcus: How about model parallelism vs tensor parallelism and kernel selection?
00:16:05 Lina: Kernel selection is influenced by layout (TP/PP). Some high-performance kernels expect a certain tensor layout. Our compile step tries permutations and picks the best. We persist that choice per model+layout.
00:16:40 Eileen: Security question — does fallback to hosted ever risk data exfiltration? We need to ensure only allowed classes of data go off-prem.
00:16:55 Samir: You control routing policy. We support header-based tagging: if a request is tagged 'sensitive' the runtime refuses spill. For hybrid, network egress is encrypted and keys never leave your HSM. We'll include network diagrams in the follow-up.
00:17:25 Rebecca: Can you share a sample pilot timeline? We want to move fast.
00:17:35 Samir: Typical pilot: week 0-1 prep (traces, infra access), week 2 deploy pilot cluster + warm graphs, week 3 run A/B (TensorRT vs vLLM) with your traces, week 4 analyze and tune. Lina will coordinate the runbook.
00:18:05 Lina: I'll propose exact dates after this call.
00:18:20 Marcus: About benchmarking — what metrics should we collect?
00:18:30 Lina: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput under sustained tail load, token-level CPU/GPU utilization, memory high-water, kernel fallback counts, graph recompile events, KV eviction counts, and output drift score.
00:19:00 Tomás: On the network side, if we use Direct Connect for hosted spill, is there an additional auth layer?
00:19:10 Samir: We support private peering and mTLS mutual auth. Additionally, we can require signed JWTs per request and support SAML/SSO for operator access.
00:19:35 Rebecca: Any recommended defaults for batch sizes to balance p95?
00:19:45 Lina: For short-response chat SLOs we keep micro-batching small (batch 1–8) with adaptive batching enabled; for throughput-heavy jobs we allow larger batch sizes. Adaptive batching looks at queue latency and will flush early to keep SLOs.
00:20:15 Marcus: Does adaptive batching play nicely with CUDA graphs?
00:20:25 Lina: It does but you need consistent shapes for graph reuse. For variable length input we use shape buckets and warm graphs per bucket. Adaptive batching triggers flushes but will prefer existing warmed graphs where possible.
00:21:00 Speaker 6: (background) How do you handle library mismatches during on-prem upgrades?
00:21:10 Theo: We provide an upgrade matrix and pinned reqs. For on-prem air-gapped installs we can provide an offline bundle. We'll include checksums in the bundle.
00:21:40 Rebecca: For the pilot can we get a smaller SLA? We're not ready for full enterprise yet.
00:21:50 Samir: Yes, pilot terms are flexible. We have a standard pilot contract.
00:22:10 Tomás: Any notes on training/inference hybrid pipelines? We sometimes fine-tune locally and serve trimmed models.
00:22:20 Lina: Fine-tuning may change operator kernels; recommend re-running the compile step and re-benchmarking warmed graphs after fine-tune. We'll help automate that in the runbook.
00:22:45 Marcus: Are there any known regression patterns when moving from fp16 to int8 quant?
00:22:55 Lina: Yes, certain softmax fusion ops and layernorm approximations can alter probabilities. We recommend targeted eval sets to detect regressions early.
00:23:30 Eileen: Compliance question: do you support audit export of per-request token logs for a window?
00:23:40 Samir: We support token-level logs for a configurable retention period; for PII you'd typically redact or avoid logging full tokens. We'll document retention options.
00:24:05 Rebecca: Ok, let's do the pilot. We'll upload traces by next Tuesday.
00:24:20 Samir: Great — we'll send the runbook and spreadsheet after the call.
00:24:35 Lina: Quick note — small transcription/typo: KV cache occasionally appears as "KV cash" in some logs; ignore that.
00:24:50 Tomás: (laughs) we've seen that.
00:25:00 Closing recap from Samir: We'll share: 1) kernel selection perf matrix, 2) triage checklist, 3) pilot runbook and helm chart, 4) security pack. Lina will setup the pilot kickoff for 2025-02-03 if Aurelius is ready.
00:25:35 Rebecca: Thanks everyone.
00:25:45 End of call.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional misattribution and minor word errors (e.g., "KV cash"). Some timestamps approximate.
